<description>
While stress-testing #36147 I noticed sporadic port collisions still occurring on FreeBSD.

`set_ephemeral_port_range()` keeps the source port out of the test port range, but only for sockets the framework creates itself. Python's `http.client` creates its sockets internally, so RPC and REST connections can still be given a source port inside the test range. A connection to a closed port can then connect to itself. For example, the wrong-RPC-port startup check failed with `BadStatusLine: POST / HTTP/1.1` because the client read back its own request.

This change adds a `netutil.HTTPConnection` subclass that sets the port range before connecting, and uses it in `AuthServiceProxy` and in the tests that open HTTP connections directly.

HTTPS is left unchanged because we don't serve RPC over TLS so it seems unnecessary.
</description>

<commits>
a2c3b1e27f test: avoid BSD ephemeral-port collisions in HTTP clients

FreeBSD and OpenBSD allocate ephemeral ports from ranges that overlap
the functional framework's fixed test ports. An outgoing localhost
connection can therefore select its destination port as its source port
and connect to itself. The wrong-RPC-port startup test exposed this on
FreeBSD as BadStatusLine: POST / HTTP/1.1, consistent with reading its
own request instead of receiving the expected connection refusal.

The existing set_ephemeral_port_range() protection only covers
explicitly created sockets.

Python's HTTP clients create their sockets internally, so apply the
helper through their connection factory before connecting. Share the
protected HTTPConnection across the RPC proxy and direct HTTP callers,
without changing system-wide settings. The HTTPS path is left alone
because bitcoind does not serve RPC over TLS.

Also adds a framework unit test checking that the option is set before
connect() for IPv4 and IPv6 on both platforms.
</commits>
